Breaking: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190m at Sotheby’s following Nazi loot claims

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that one of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record.
  • In a recent development, but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates.
  • Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across New York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

In a recent development, but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in Fresh York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across New York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s announced that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

According to recent reports, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's.

Sources indicate that estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Acquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

According to recent reports, soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s Upcoming York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Industry observers note that ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

Recent findings suggest that the subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

The top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

Recent findings suggest that harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's.

Sources indicate that one of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

Mary Cassatt also established a fresh auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

According to recent reports, only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

Inside Maker's Mark brand identity by Turner Duckworth

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (350 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Maker's Mark brand identity around its red wax, casting Star Hill Farm materials into marks that tell the story.
  • Recent findings suggest that the bottle does the talking.
  • Sources indicate that the type comes from a person, not a library.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Maker's Mark brand identity around its red wax, casting Star Hill Farm materials into marks that tell the story.

Recent findings suggest that the bottle does the talking. Turner Duckworth kept the hand-dipped red top exactly where it belongs, at the center of the system, then built a whole language out of it. Wheat stalks, oak rings and native flora from Star Hill Farm were dipped and cast in the same red wax, so the marks that carry the brand are literal pieces of the place. Against a Wheat Cream ground, the red reads as one loud note in a quiet room, with Printmaker's Black holding the type steady.

Sources indicate that the type comes from a person, not a library. Co-founder Margie Samuels shaped the original bottle, and the studio recreated her handwriting as a custom typeface with Nick Cooke at G-Type. Hundreds of characters, contextual alternates and ligatures keep it feeling handwritten rather than set, and her voice runs through the labels, menus and posters in a flowing, wax-like hand.

Layouts stay plain on purpose. A letterhead puts the Samuels family's SIV mark at the center and the distillery address in the corner, so place sits at the heart of every sheet. Type stays large and calm, with room around it, and the wordmark does its work without decoration.

The palette is the bottle, remembered in three tones. Wheat Cream is the ground, true to the label. Printmaker's Black carries the type. Wax Red does the rest, in finish and in form: powder-coated metal, glazing and varnish applied to objects with smooth, flowing shapes. The same red runs across mugs, folders, books and table tents, so every object in the world feels dipped from the same pot.

According to recent reports, scott Grummett photographed the world at Star Hill Farm in warm cream tones and natural light, with touches of glossy wax red. The pictures tell the slower story behind the liquid: hand-rotated barrels, hand-cut labels, hand-dipped bottles, and the land that gives it flavour.

Industry News: Iraq’s national museum introduces reopening after major renovations

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December.
  • Recent findings suggest that several important artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry.
  • The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the latest government under Ali al-Zaidi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several newly introduced galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Recent findings suggest that several important artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The new Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.

The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the latest government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are aims afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an key moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.

Recent findings suggest that according to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.

According to recent reports, A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while new ones been revealed. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.

Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has unveiled that a latest museum will open in the former Presidential Palace in Babylon Photo: Hadani Ditmars.

Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.

Industry observers note that al-Dakhili has also confirmed that the openings of three latest museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement indicates.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”.

In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.

Alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, states: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a fresh national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”.

Artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, says the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.

It has been revealed that charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he notes. “The biggest matter seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”.

Recent findings suggest that the CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report says.

According to recent reports, UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”.

It has been revealed that kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, claims: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.

“Focused giving” may be partly the answer says the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a upcoming Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

According to recent reports, picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

According to recent reports, here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

The primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. If you have the Amex Gold, Platinum, or a no-annual-fee Amex Everyday card earning MR points, you can transfer directly to Hawaiian. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so plan accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

This means your primary accumulation strategy is transfer partners — Amex MR and Bilt are your best levers.

According to recent reports, another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

According to recent reports, finally, the no fuel surcharges policy is a genuine differentiator. HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. What you see is what you get.

Enter your route — for example, HNL to OGG (Honolulu to Kahului, Maui) or HNL to LIH (Honolulu to Lihue, Kauai). Plug in your desired travel date and search. But you will get a reliable, on-time carrier, clean aircraft, and the undeniable satisfaction of hopping between two of the most beautiful island destinations on Earth without opening your wallet at the gate.

Recent findings suggest that for the ChooseFI traveler, the win isn't the in-flight experience — it's the mental accounting shift. Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has announced that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its fresh director from July 2027.

Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he said he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.

It has been revealed that “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”.

The Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.

In a recent development, this success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.

Sources indicate that but Gruijthuijsen noted he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he says. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”.

Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.

It has been revealed that from one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental demonstrates of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he says.

From the Finns, he will also bring an key lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he says: “Less talking, more doing.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentagram drew a full custom alphabet for Storefront Gala 2026, turning the Oyster Bar sign into loud, blocky, crayon-bright type.

Sources indicate that the gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL. Anyone who has eaten under those Guastavino vaults knows the sign on the wall. Rudolph de Harak packed its letters tight, rimmed them in heavy black outlines, and filled them with colors straight out of a crayon box. Against wood paneling and old tile, it has always looked like the one guest in the room who came to have fun. Pentagram started from a simple question: what would the rest of that alphabet look like?

The answer is a custom display typeface with a full set of letters and numerals. Strokes run broad, corners clip short, and counters turn angular. The O is an octagon with a diamond punched through its middle, and that shape sets the rules for every other character. Blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple take turns filling the forms.

Storefront Gala 2026 appears in compact stacks and stepped arrangements, with rotated numerals adding an unexpected twist. Letters meet along their black outlines and lock into continuous compositions that feel assembled from colorful building blocks. A smaller sans serif organizes the event information around these expressive forms, holding the honorees, the venue, and the date in quiet lines above the noise.

Recent findings suggest that the system runs across digital announcements, posters, a folded program, screen graphics, and embroidered caps. Some pieces set the colored letters on white, while others flood the ground with a single saturated color and let the type push back. The folded program carries the full stack in a run of blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple, with the small sans serif keeping the facts straight at the top of the sheet.

Industry observers note that the caps are the most tactile piece of the set, the lettering stitched small across white, green, and pale blue cotton. An orange sign stands on the tiled floor, and the word SALOON stretches across a wood doorway in the same blocky letters, proof the alphabet holds its shape from a poster down to a doorway. Pentagram has designed identities for Storefront since 2012, and this one plays the longest with the room it was made for.

Industry News: The Filmmakers Behind ‘Primetime’ Printed the Entire Movie on 16mm and Rescanned It

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Primetime, a feature film about Chris Hansen and his hit TV show To Catch a Predator, keeps viewers gripped not just by the intense story brought to life by actors Robert Pattinson and Merritt Wever, but by the striking cinematography.
  • One of the biggest reasons for its distinct filmic look is that director Lance Oppenheim and cinematographer David Bolen opted to shoot the majority of the movie on an Alexa 35 before printing it onto a 16mm Kodak 50D and rescanning it to 6K, a process known as digital-to-film-to-digital.
  • Writing for American Cinematographer, Bolen explains that he shot most of the film at 6400 ISO to “add as much noise and texture as I could.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Primetime, a feature film about Chris Hansen and his hit TV show To Catch a Predator, keeps viewers gripped not just by the intense story brought to life by actors Robert Pattinson and Merritt Wever, but by the striking cinematography.

One of the biggest reasons for its distinct filmic look is that director Lance Oppenheim and cinematographer David Bolen opted to shoot the majority of the movie on an Alexa 35 before printing it onto a 16mm Kodak 50D and rescanning it to 6K, a process known as digital-to-film-to-digital.

Writing for American Cinematographer, Bolen explains that he shot most of the film at 6400 ISO to “add as much noise and texture as I could.”.

It has been revealed that the crew used London-based Cinelab, which has a third-generation 16mm Cine-Mitchell recorder built in-house. Once the film print was created, it was scanned back into digital using an Arriscan, which delivers “perfect edge-to-edge focus.” The resulting footage was then regraded.

Recent findings suggest that “Primetime is also a period film, in a way, and working with the film print helped make the visuals far more immersive,” says Bolen. “Any feeling of artifice in the image seemed to disappear after printing to film.”.

However, the film wasn’t shot entirely with the digital-to-film-to-digital method: Oppenheim and Bolen utilized a few obscure, frankly bizarre, cameras as they searched for a way to recreate that early 2000s aesthetic and also communicate the plot to the audience.

Sources indicate that one such camera was a 2005 MiniDV camera, the Panasonic AG DVX 100B. Bolen used this for the hidden camera shots, and it is a very similar technology that was used to film the original show, To Catch a Predator.

Recent findings suggest that “These cameras are a challenge, because unlike modern cinema cameras, they can’t shoot in a LOG color space,” Bolen notes. “We didn’t really alter their baseline settings; we decided to lean into the cameras’ built-in contrast. To Catch a Predator has such a strong look, and we tried to match it as closely as possible in-camera. Even in the final grade, we made very few adjustments.”.

Recent findings suggest that but that distinct look posed a problem in the editing room: how to blend the shots taken by different cameras together. After all, DV cameras are not cinematic.

In a recent development, “We couldn’t get them to match,” states Bolen on the Mark Bone YouTube channel. “Like, no matter what we did with the settings, some would skew red, some would skew green, on some the exposure seemed off.”.

But Oppenheim didn’t care and threw the rules out of the window. In fact, he would film the same scenes on different cameras, and then in the edit, choose whichever one he liked.

Speaking of other cameras, there were two more that Oppenheim and Bolen used: a Plumbicon tube camera and a medical camera — the kind used for colonoscopies.

Archer Green points out that the Plumbicon tube camera actually dates back to the 1980s.

Industry observers note that “It was meant to serve as a ‘spiritual’ camera rather than a period-accurate one,” Bolen writes for American Cinematographer. “These cameras use vacuum RGB tubes that split light into red, green, and blue, and the beautiful thing is that the tubes age and burn out over time. In a way, it’s a camera that feels like it has a soul — it decays over time, just like a human does.”.

The creators of ‘PRIMETIME’ explain how they shot a scene using a 480p colonoscopy camera 🎥🤯https://t.co/Z8m4aT7YM0.

— Complex Pop Culture (@ComplexPop) September 27, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that for one of the close-ups of Pattinson, Bolen used a doctor’s colonoscopy camera. The crew even built a rig to hammer home the effect.

“That was a scary one because that camera does shoot 480p and I was like, ‘How am I going to get this approved?’ But to A24’s credit [the film distributor], they were like, ‘this is awesome’,” Bolen says.

“There are no rules. We don’t have to shoot 6K. 480p looks awesome on the massive screen; I love it. It’s my favorite part of the movie.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Version 3.4, which is available starting today, promises to maximize the viewfinder when the iPhone Duo is unfolded.
  • Recent findings suggest that “On the outer screen, we’ve added a few new modes, including a viewfinder preview and flash-fill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that halide has announced version 3.4, much of which focuses on optimizations for the iPhone Duo. This includes a new “XL” mode that is designed for two-handed operation, as well as a feature that doesn’t avoid the crease, but instead embraces it.

Version 3.4, which is available starting today, promises to maximize the viewfinder when the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Halide indicates this feature, called XL mode, allows for “powerful two-handed operation.”.

Recent findings suggest that “On the outer screen, we’ve added a few new modes, including a viewfinder preview and flash-fill. In low-light, the latter gives you a softer alternative to the built-in flash,” Halide adds.

In a recent development, “While apps like Apple’s own camera app expand the viewfinder to take up the full screen, it’s impossible to do this without obstructing your shot with camera controls. That poses a challenge when composing shots, so we’ve taken the approach of keeping the viewfinder clean.”.

Recent findings suggest that beyond just making these changes that take advantage of the two form factors the Duo offers, Halide went one step further and specifically engineered an interface for when the Duo is half-folded. The company says that while most are avoiding the crease that appears when the phone is folded, it went the opposite way and embraced it.

Sources indicate that “Back when the iPhone X rolled out in 2017, we were the first app to ’embraced the notch’ by putting histograms in the ears of the phone. Today, we think we’re the first app to ’embrace the crease,’ placing the histograms in the fold, an otherwise no-man’s-land of interactions,” Halide indicates.

By default, Halide’s camera controls sit on the same side as the camera itself. Tapping the arrows in the sidebar, the left and right sides swap, turning Halide into a waist level viewfinder.

Halide provided a few sample images taken with the updated Duo app:.

Halide usually doesn’t take long to patch its app when new hardware lands, and even though the interface for this Duo-specific update feels like it should have taken a lot longer, it really isn’t too far off from what Halide provided for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro launch. When it dropped version 3.2, which gave support for variable aperture control, that arrived on October 2, which is about three weeks after the iPhone 18 Pro landed on store shelves. This update for the Duo comes just shy of a month after the Duo launched on October 23.

Halide version 3.4 is available starting today.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar.
  • “At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, remarked at the end of the evening.
  • Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, remarked at the end of the evening.

Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

Hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

Emily Carr, Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure), around 1912 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

Jean Paul Riopelle, Herbeuse, 1967 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

According to recent reports, A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

According to recent reports, among the night’s other major-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

Paul-Émile Borduas, Empâtement, 1957 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

Arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a newly introduced auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

Ivan Eyre, Golden Rod, 1981 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ACDSee Photo Studio has confirmed version 27, which brings a bunch of latest features, including several powered by AI, perhaps elevating the tool to the level of Adobe’s offerings.

Version 27 of the photo management and editing software for macOS introduces generative AI tools for creating and editing images, along with AI-powered organization that the tech giant says can find and group photos together by how they look. These newly introduced options don’t compromise non-destructive editing, either.

In short, ACDSee has embraced AI editing.

According to recent reports, “AI is shaping the future of photography and it’s our goal to lead the way in that space,” Frank Lin, CTO of ACD Systems, claims. “With ACDSee Photo Studio for Mac 27, we’re bringing generative AI directly into the creative process, making it easier to find, organize and transform images while giving photographers the flexibility and control they need to bring their vision to life.”.

The bulk of the updates to version 27 are AI-focused, with the top-billed latest feature having the highest chance of being the most controversial: image generation.

“Turn a text prompt into an image, choose a preset visual effect, or bring in reference images to guide character, style, and composition, right inside the photo workflow,” ACDSee says. AI generation isn’t fresh for photography tools, as Photoshop has had it for years now, but it’s not necessarily something that photographers are specifically asking for in a Lightroom competitor. Still, it’s here now.

It has been revealed that ACDSee appears to be following Adobe’s lead with the next feature, as it now supports editing via prompting. Photographers can describe a change in plain language or “use reference images to guide the look, and reshape a photo without a single brush stroke.”.

Recent findings suggest that the AI search tool looks to be an alternative to Excire Photo and will find photos visually related to any primary target, with no keywords or tagging required. Images can also be grouped by similarity.

ACDSee Photo Studio for Mac 27 is available for $119.99, including 10,000 AI Credits for generative AI tools and 100GB of cloud storage.

Latest Update: This iPhone App Lets You Take Photos By Clapping

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.
  • HyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment.
  • Meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.

HyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment. For example, when photographing sports, children, or pets, the app can trip the shutter as soon as motion appears in the frame.

Meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot. Customers can customize the sensitivity for the app and the delay between detection and shooting.

Recent findings suggest that the app’s original purpose, which remains a core focus, was to make it easier to photograph lightning. It can use sound for this as well, though thunder arrives well after the flash of lightning itself. The app can also trigger a shot when it detects a sudden surge of light hitting the camera.

It has been revealed that hyperCam can also trigger the shutter under other conditions, including camera shake, such as when the iPhone moves or tilts, or complete stability, such as when it is mounted on a tripod. Additionally, it can capture timelapse photos when it detects changes in light or motion, or wait to fire until someone in the frame smiles.

Lightning triggers are not a new concept in photography. Photographers with DSLRs and mirrorless cameras have been using them for years, and new ones hit the market every so often, like the Bolt Hunter earlier this year.

Lightning triggers rely on the same principle as HyperCam: it is simply impossible for a photographer to manually press the shutter fast enough to catch fleeting events like lightning. Photographers can certainly try and can improve their odds by firing off long, rapid bursts of frames. However, assistance is required for consistent success.

HyperCam Trigger is available now in the App Store for free.

However, some features are locked behind a paywall, including subject filters, short event video recording with frame extraction, detection zones, longer pre-trigger buffers, longer bursts, RAW recording, HDR, and more. HyperCam Pro is available for $3.99 per month, $22.99 per year, or $44.99 for lifetime access.

Breaking: Apple’s Camera and Photo Software Lead Jon McCormack Has Retired

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired.
  • Industry observers note that bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October.
  • Update 11/20 @ 8 AM: McCormack shared this story on his Instagram, perhaps subtly confirming its accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired. A spectacular photographer in his own right, McCormack is stepping away, and his departure signals a major change for Apple regardless of the circumstances.

Industry observers note that bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October. This information has not been independently verified, as at the time of publication, neither Apple nor McCormack has confirmed his departure.

Update 11/20 @ 8 AM: McCormack shared this story on his Instagram, perhaps subtly confirming its accuracy.

McCormack, who was Apple’s vice president of camera and photo engineering, has been a major figure at the Silicon Valley giant since he arrived there in 2018. He oversaw the development of not only the iPhone camera system but also the camera software and all of the computational features that go along with it.

It has been revealed that he was present for every briefing and discussion about the iPhone camera system through that time and became personally known to everyone at PetaPixel. He is also regularly quoted speaking about Apple’s philosophy regarding cameras and photography.

“Here’s our view of what a photograph is: The way we like to think of it is that it’s a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened,” he told PetaPixel back in 2024, just as generative AI was beginning its steady march into the creative industry. Apple has, since then, largely stayed that course.

Perhaps most importantly, McCormack is actually a photographer. In April, PetaPixel featured his most recent book, titled “Patterns: Art of the Natural World.”.

It has been revealed that “I grew up on a farm in the Outback, Queensland in Australia,” McCormack said. “Sheep and cattle property. We had no full-time electricity. We had a 32-volt generator that dad would run at night so that a little 12-inch black and white TV could be a thing. This is also when I got my first camera, my hand-me-down camera, and it wasn’t even my dad’s hand-me-down camera. It was my grandfather’s, a Minolta 35mm Mark IV made in either 1949 or 1950. I still have it.”.

His series made it abundantly clear that McCormack cares deeply about nature.

“My goal here is for people to look at our planet like a Fabergé egg,” McCormack explained. “It is unique, one of them in existence. It’s fragile, it’s intricate, it’s beautiful. It’s something to be protected and taken care of, and it’s something you can fall in love with.”.

Sources indicate that it’s hard to think of a greater loss for Apple than McCormack. It is unlikely that Apple will find someone who is nearly as talented or who cares as much about photography as a fine art. PetaPixel is hard-pressed to believe there was anyone better for his role at the manufacturer than he was.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With more creators capturing both photos and videos, accessory makers are stepping up to meet the demand.
  • Photographers often like ball heads because they are versatile, easy to adjust, and stable.
  • “Today, the line between photography and videography is becoming increasingly blurred.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With more creators capturing both photos and videos, accessory makers are stepping up to meet the demand. Heipi’s new 2-in-1 hybrid tripod head for photo and video promises the best of both worlds.

Photographers often like ball heads because they are versatile, easy to adjust, and stable. By loosening the head, photographers can quickly recompose their shots. However, ball heads are not as easy to control or as smooth for panning motion as a traditional pan-tilt fluid head, which videographers typically prefer. Further, Heipi notes its fresh head also delivers the balancing performance of a gimbal head, a popular choice for wildlife and birding photographers with huge, heavy lenses.

“Today, the line between photography and videography is becoming increasingly blurred. During a single shoot, creators may switch between wide-angle and telephoto lenses, move from still photography to video, and capture a wider range of perspectives and moments,” Heipi writes on Kickstarter. “Yet different shooting needs often call for different support equipment: a ball head, a gimbal head, a fluid head, and more. Carrying multiple heads adds bulk to your gear and extra weight to every journey.”.

Heipi believes its fresh hybrid head offers all the benefits of separate tripod heads in a single package.

Industry observers note that the Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head weighs 560 grams (just over 1.2 pounds) and is about the size of a traditional ball head. However, it can instantly switch from ball head mode to pan-tilt mode, and videographers can screw on a grip for even more control.

Industry observers note that heipi’s fresh tripod head also features a stepless counterbalance system designed for gear weighing from 1.5 to 5 kilograms (3.3 to 11 pounds). That encompasses a wide range of equipment, including those substantial, heavy supertelephoto lenses mentioned earlier.

The KB50 features a standard 3/8″-16 UNC female thread on its base, allowing it to attach to a wide variety of tripod legs. It also includes an Arca-Swiss clamp.

The Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head is available to back on Kickstarter now, starting at $428, which is a $120 discount compared to the $548 MSRP. Heipi claims it will begin shipping in April 2027. With just over 40 days left in the campaign, Heipi has already shattered its $10,000 goal.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees).
  • It has been revealed that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%.
  • Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

It has been revealed that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Recent findings suggest that business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Sources indicate that price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

In a recent development, still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a fresh home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

In a recent development, A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of important 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

Illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

It has been revealed that gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in New York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

In a recent development, gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in Latest York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a upcoming auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

It has been revealed that though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

The appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime New York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

Recent findings suggest that among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

Large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Sources indicate that measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and important champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

It has been revealed that the evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the New York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

Industry observers note that apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca remarked. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

Smith & Diction rebuilt the PHS brand identity around a Bloom logo, with three plants growing from the letters and Philadelphia grid underneath.

According to recent reports, the old mark was a tree in a circle, and it mentioned too little about an organization that does far more than plant trees. The Pennsylvania Horticultural Society tends gardens and parks across the Philadelphia region and runs the Flower Show. The new mark keeps the letters PHS as the foundation and grows three plants out of them, each drawn by Summer McClure to fit a Philadelphia city block. In deep green and burgundy on cream, mint, and sky blue, with dozens of colors in the palette, the identity looks like a garden because it behaves like one: every visit highlights something new.

The wordmark is custom, built to hold the plants like roots hold a stem. The supporting type comes from the societyâs own archive: old exhibition posters that were beautiful and hardworking, no frills, just type. Caslon Doric leads, with the confidence and clean legibility of classic newspaper headlines, and ES Park backs it up, a slab serif with geometric moments and measured softness.

Underneath it all sits William Pennâs original city grid. The studio baked the grid into the logo itself, then extended it through every print layout, matching the grid to the width of the flowers. Like beds in a garden, the structure keeps everything in place while each layout keeps its own personality. The mark never sits still: Henrique Barone hand-drew every frame of the plants growing, and Justin Lawes made a version that sways with the breeze.

Recent findings suggest that this is a brand made to be held, not just seen. The studio printed a 42-page brand book, made a matte gold lapel pin of the mark, and built a flip book that indicates the logo growing frame by frame. They matched paper tones to nearly every brand color, so the team can print in-house and stay on brand. The book cover carries the Bloom logo in dark green on mint, with an orange seal.

The floral illustrations do more than decorate. Each one stands for a part of the organization: a flower in a cocktail glass for the Pop Up Gardens, a leafy radish for the community gardens, an oak leaf for the Healthy Neighborhoods program, a branching tree for the McLean Library. The library also gives the 2027 Philadelphia Flower Show its own peony mark, while Bre Furlongâs photographs of 18 flowers, including the tulip the studio calls the Ballerina, carry the ICONIC theme in Herbus type.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Associated Press is moving eight photo editor positions to India today, in a move condemned by unions.
  • Industry observers note that the roles are currently carried out in the United States, but today is their last day.
  • “AP is at it again,” the AP News Guild wrote on X last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Associated Press is moving eight photo editor positions to India today, in a move condemned by unions.

Industry observers note that the roles are currently carried out in the United States, but today is their last day. The offshoring follows similar moves this summer, when AP laid off 20 video production jobs in the U.S. and moved them to its hub in Noida, India.

“AP is at it again,” the AP News Guild wrote on X last week. “The News Media Guild learned Monday that AP will offshore eight photo positions after already gutting its U.S. video production team.”.

In a statement, the News Media Guild president Kimberlee Krusei called AP’s move “union busting.”.

“Fewer people, fewer communities being covered, and less news. That’s the impact of today’s decision,” says Krusei. “AP’s newsgathering has gone beyond ‘lean’ to leaving many coverage areas abandoned. The remaining journalists are asked to do the impossible and it highlights.”.

The Guild indicates that far from just picking photos taken by AP photographers, the editors provide direction, guide the photographers, correct essential information, and scrutinize images for alterations.

“They bring decades of local knowledge, news judgment and connections. They negotiate with outside photographers to buy the rights to photos — a now essential part of covering breaking news.”.

One of the affected photo editors, Pablo Salinas, who is based in Latest York, says that he went above and beyond in 2019 when he obtained the rights to a shocking photo of a drowned father and daughter lying face down in the Rio Grande River.

Sources indicate that “That was a picture that I don’t think any other photo editor would have been able to get,” indicates Salinas. “Because it wasn’t ours, I scoured social media and found it and got in touch with the photographer. And she reluctantly gave us permission to use it.”.

The photo went viral and became part of the story about the border crisis.

“AP benefits from having photo editors that are local to where the news is being produced,” says AP photographer Matt Rourke.

“It’s a partnership,” adds Salinas. “The kind of partnership you lose when you sacrifice these jobs to save a few dollars.”.

Photo editors are intimately involved in the biggest stories of the day. They might be working closely with local photographers to move hundreds of shots illustrating crucial election results. Or securing the rights to sensitive images that convey difficult news. AP’s Pablo Salinas went in front of the camera to talk about the partnership that’s lost when news leaders sacrifice jobs like his. Tell the firm their valuable work can’t just be done from anywhere at this link: https://t.co/euBigYM1tt.

— AP News Guild (@APNewsGuild) November 12, 2026.

An AP spokesperson tells TheWrap that the agency is respecting and following the collective bargaining agreement.

“This is part of the changes we confirmed over the summer to significantly scale our visual production capabilities at our new hub in Noida, India, where we have added dozens of talented journalists to our global news organization,” the spokesperson says.

The AP says that its hub in Noida will soon employ nearly 100 video producers and photo editors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thypoch has announced its first autofocus prime lens, the $349 AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor for Fujifilm X mount.

Editor’s Note: This article originally appeared on PetaPixel on October 27. Multiple outlets including B&H Photo listed the lens, but Thypoch changed the release date after publication. As a courtesy, PetaPixel agreed to adjust the publish date to November 20. The content of this story is unchanged.

In a recent development, with its approximately 35mm equivalent focal length, Thypoch’s first autofocus lens for Fujifilm X mount and first autofocus prime lens period is well-suited to a wide range of photographic applications. The 35mm focal length is a classic one for a reason. It works well for street, landscapes, portraits, and travel, to name a few go-to genres.

Thypoch has long been associated with classically-inspired manual focus lenses, like the Simera 50mm f/1.4 and Ksana 21mm f/3.5. However, the manufacturer’s vibe changed considerably when it released its first autofocus lens, the Voyager 24-50mm f/2.8 for full-frame Sony E-mount cameras.

The fresh Thypoch AF 23mm f/1.4 Sculptor is styled much like the Voyager, with diagonal lines and a vintage-inspired yet modern design. Although beauty is subjective, the Sculptor will likely earn a few fans thanks to its handsome looks.

In a recent development, it's ultimately what's on the inside that counts, though. Inside the Sculptor, 12 lens elements are arranged across ten groups, promising edge-to-edge sharpness even at the maximum f/1.4 aperture. A 10-bladed aperture diaphragm sits behind the glass.

Recent findings suggest that the lens is also quite compact, measuring just 71.4 millimeters (2.8 inches) long with a 52mm front filter thread. The lens weighs 283 grams (just under 10 ounces).

Recent findings suggest that the autofocus prime can focus as close as 0.25 meters (0.82 feet), giving a maximum magnification of about 0.13x. It's definitely not a macro lens.

The Sculptor's most obvious competitor is Fujifilm's own XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WR lens, which costs $1,049.95. Fujifilm's lens weighs 375 grams (13.2 ounces) and is 77.8 millimeters (3.1 inches) long. Thypoch's new lens is much lighter and more affordable.

Fujifilm XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WRBuy latest on B&HFujifilm XF 23mm f/1.4 R LM WRBuy used on KEH.comSigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN ContemporaryBuy new on B&HSigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN ContemporaryBuy used on KEH.com.

Recent findings suggest that another competitor is the Sigma 23mm f/1.4 DC DN Contemporary. It's $609 right now thanks to a $50 discount and is generally well respected. It weighs 340 grams (12 ounces) and is 76.9 millimeters (three inches) long. Again, heavier than Thypoch's newly introduced lens by a decent margin.

Then there's the TTArtisan 23mm f/1.4 lens, which costs just $113.99. There's a significant catch, though, as TTArtisan's lens is manual focus only. It is extremely compact, measuring just 40.5 millimeters (1.6 inches) long. It weighs about 230 grams (8.1 ounces).

Industry observers note that the Thypoch Sculptor AF 23mm f/1.4 should ship soon. It's available to preorder now for $349. It's the most affordable autofocus-equipped 23mm f/1.4 prime lens for Fujifilm X-mount cameras, and the lightest AF lens of its kind for the system. It will likely attract significant attention among Fujifilm camera owners.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A drone operator filmed English soccer team Manchester United’s first training session with new coach Mauricio Pochettino and shared the “unethical” footage on YouTube.
  • men’s national soccer team (USMNT) to become head coach of English Premier League club Manchester United.
  • According to recent reports, however, a drone operator who runs the YouTube account CC Overview — which describes itself as sharing “drone footage of construction at football stadia and events affecting our environment” — flew his aerial device over the facility during Pochettino’s first training session.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A drone operator filmed English soccer team Manchester United’s first training session with new coach Mauricio Pochettino and shared the “unethical” footage on YouTube.

Pochettino officially left the U.S. men’s national soccer team (USMNT) to become head coach of English Premier League club Manchester United. On Thursday, he oversaw his first training session with Man United’s first-team squad ahead of Sunday’s Premier League game against Liverpool at the club’s Carrington training ground.

According to recent reports, however, a drone operator who runs the YouTube account CC Overview — which describes itself as sharing “drone footage of construction at football stadia and events affecting our environment” — flew his aerial device over the facility during Pochettino’s first training session. He then posted a 12-minute segment on YouTube on Thursday.

Sources indicate that according to a report by The Athletic, Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, were identifiable in the aerial footage, which amassed over 600,000 views on YouTube. The footage demonstrated Pochettino leading a training session with one group of players, while his assistant Jesus Perez oversaw two separate groups. The video, filmed at United’s Carrington training base, also captured audio of the YouTuber apparently controlling the drone saying “let’s get closer,” before zooming in on the upcoming head coach.

It has been revealed that the drone operator has since apologized for a “total error in judgment.” He states the aerial footage was legal under U.K. drone laws but has removed the “unethical” video from YouTube.

“A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Man United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part,” the drone operator writes in a post on YouTube.

According to recent reports, the drone operator describes aiming to film Pochettino in the club’s training kit for the first time, but adds he had no intention of recording a “meaningful training session.” The YouTuber indicates he was operating under an incorrect assumption that it was open to media outlets. He also insists he acted independently and was not working on behalf of Liverpool or any other football club.

“I would like to apologize to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match,” the drone operator notes.

Man United prohibits the use of drones at its Carrington training facility, where signs warn that anyone operating a drone could face civil action or prosecution.

In the U.K., capturing aerial footage using drones is permitted provided operators comply with Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) safety regulations, as well as privacy and data protection laws.

CAA guidance on privacy for drone use details: “If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you’re likely to be breaking data protection laws.” It adds that drone operators should “let people know before you start recording or taking pictures”.
