In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators.
  • In a recent development, the three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners.
  • Industry observers note that upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators. A security guard directed me to the 14th floor of the 1950s office building, where drop ceilings, an exposed HVAC system, and two people I assumed were the exhibition organizers dressed in corporate drag greeted me. They quickly clarified they were not; they were from AmTrustRE, the real estate firm that offered the derelict 23,000-square-foot office space to the artists for free while preparing it — and three other unoccupied floors — for their next corporate tenants.

In a recent development, the three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners. On view through this Sunday, November 22, the show arrives just as the Whitney Museum of American Art opens artport: A History of Internet Art, signaling a newly introduced wave of institutional recognition for internet-grown art. With 260 Madison artists Maya Man, Rachel Rossin, and Eva and Franco Mattes among those included in the Whitney’s 25th-anniversary exhibition for its net art commissioning platform, the Midtown show feels especially urgent, if only because it takes place at the precipice of a paradigmatic shift within the art world.

Industry observers note that upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device. Titled “It Takes a Global Village Idiot” (2018) after philosopher Marshall McLuhan’s early ’60s theory that information-age technology “recreates the world in the image of a global village,” the sculpture forces viewers to confront the fact that the quick fixes of amusement proffered by technology rely on the same methods of data extraction that undergird systemic violence. It’s an unsettling introduction to a show where, even in its more humorous, delusionally conspiratorial, or enchanting moments, discomfort is always in the periphery.

Sources indicate that “We don’t want to make a show or art that tries to be some form of escapism,” Rogríguez told Hyperallergic during an interview the week after the opening. “It’s like the [Werner Herzog] quote, ‘The poet must not avert his eyes.’ If some art in the show seems depressing, it’s because we live in what seems a depressing time.”.

In a recent development, rodríguez and Matasheva, who are also a couple, began making work together seven years ago while studying film in Montreal. Their video-art duo is named after Olivier Assayas’s 2002 film Demonlover, where multiple global corporations compete for a fresh immersive Japanese hentai firm through extreme methods of espionage, exploitation, and blackmail.

“DemonLovers is about the libidinal economy and how algorithms are weaponizing our very basic instincts and desires,” Matasheva told Hyperallergic, echoing Rodríguez’s interest in what he calls “financial Freud,” or the psychoanalytic dimension of digital capital flows.

It has been revealed that both DemonLovers’s own two works in the show and those they curated certainly don’t shy away from the degradation associated with extractive economies, be it of the self, physical infrastructure, or the proverbial global village. Nearby Kessler’s work, Theresa Tomi Faison’s “The Long Tail” (2026) climbs up one of the floor’s load-bearing columns. Across the curved sculpture’s six screens, images of memes, forum screenshots, and phrases ruminating on contemporary capital flow all accumulate and dissolve downstream. The river of digital spam ends at the viewer’s feet, inculcating the audience, but also the space itself, which the curators characterize as shaped by "junkspace” — architect Rem Koolhaas's term for fallout that “remains after modernization has run its course.”.

Among works that are either readymades or play with the form’s history — including Anthony Discenza’s windowsill pile of unopened credit card and loan offer letters in “Offers” (2026) and Eva and Franco Mattes’s distended taxidermied cat, “Longcat” (2026) — the corporate detritus can be difficult to parse from the artistic interventions. At one point, I mistook a few square feet of wallpaper with the Champion logo for a latest work. The curators clarified during a later conversation that it was actually kept from the office’s previous tenants, HanesBrands, which owns Champion.

According to recent reports, having also inherited the space’s trove of gutted bathrooms, broken drywall, and stripped concrete floors (in short, its junkspace), the curators mentioned they view 260 Madison through “layers of site responsiveness” more than anything. With some works, that connection emerged during the eleventh hour of installation. With others, the site occasioned the work itself. Ivana Dama used exposed air vents for “The Air Was Already Here” (2026), a sound work that channels air through reeds, transforming the invisible, inaudible rhythms of the space into what the artist describes as a “sculptural presence.” Pictures Generation artist Matt Mullican took a 47-foot span of unused wall space as an opportunity to reflect on his five-decade practice of constructing, deconstructing, and classifying systems of representation and perception with largely nonverbal symbols.

“He spent three days here drawing his entire practice on the wall, right from the beginning to the end,” Matasheva remarked regarding Mullican’s monumental graphite piece, “Representing The Work” (2026). “He said he will give a lecture about it and that it's a very key work for him. It's kind of a conclusion of his practice.”.

Meanwhile, the show’s video works are lodged into broken columns, ceiling alcoves, liminal backrooms, bathroom plumbing, abstract paintings, and even a hanging pink punching bag, a veritable reunion of the last decade of post-internet art movements. Alumni from Joshua Citarella’s publishing platform Do Not Research, the New Museum-affiliated Rhizome, and the traveling video and film screening series Open Secret, including Faison, Dana Dawud, Yehwan Song, and Ruba Al-Sweel, have contributed works. Many of them feature themes of surveillance, internet-induced conspiracy, and social media performance, as well as the technological, often AI-abetted methods of production that have come to define such enclaves.

Yet, for all the immateriality and speculative knowledge that flows through these works, 260 Madison equally plumbs an idea of technology with a long, craft-driven history. Tabak, a sculptor with a background in furniture design, is the driving force behind this facet of the show — and the currents of divination, enchantment, and even sublimity that come with it.

Industry observers note that “My practice is very handmade and material-focused, so I always know that that’s what I would contribute to the curatorial vision,” Tabak told Hyperallergic. “And just being in Midtown, you shouldn’t separate a show from what’s happening around it.

According to recent reports, tabak was particularly interested in curating works that “blur the line between the hand and technology,” inviting artists who “haven’t had a lot of chances to show in art contexts, whether it’s because they are in the design world or have nine-to-fives,” to participate in the exhibition. She explains that many of them complicate the very notion of technology and its use, citing Brian Oakes’s “Vessel 9” (2025), which gathers 3D-modeled circuit boards into a suspended “techno-Gothic” chandelier, and Ryan Decker’s “The Wavemaker Falters” (2026), which uses a motorized, rudder-like instrument to swoosh water through a raised vessel resembling a spaceship.

It has been revealed that “We view technology not as something that has arrived in the 20th century, but something that has made humanity possible,” Matasheva said, expanding on Tabak’s comment. “Language is a technology, a chisel is a technology, everything is a technology.”.

Sources indicate that while many of the show’s craft-driven works conjure the anthropologist Alfred Gell’s idea that art is a technology that enchants, and in turn, becomes enchanted, others wield technology in the service of care. Kylie Mitchell repurposes a light-seeking solar robot and discarded electronic parts to move a found bird’s nest and egg toward a life-sustaining heat lamp. A few dozen feet away, Gregory Kalliche’s installation “Black-tailed gull nest; Ring-necked Pheasant Nest; Mallard Nest” (2016) suspends an LED light over three metal folding chairs printed with images of bird egg nests. Ben Gould’s “Ark II” (2026), on the other hand, augments a hospital gurney with eight aluminum armatures that hold fresh red roses inside coil-shaped glass vials. Doubling as a literal manifestation of Shakespeare’s “this mortal coil” phrase in Hamlet, the sculpture’s sterile infrastructure butts against the transitory visual comfort proffered by its flowers, mirroring a healthcare ecosystem wherein privatization, optimization, and tech automation have whittled medicine’s promises of care, healing, and empathy into mere aesthetic veneers.

It’s no coincidence that many of the works in 260 Madison position technology as both a pathogen and cure for today’s cultural ailments. In fact, when the real estate developers initially contacted Columbia University’s School of the Arts, it was to invite artists to “activate” a 36,000-square-foot gutted Duane Reade on the building’s ground floor. The developers eventually retracted their offer and moved the exhibition to the 14th floor, citing ongoing construction. Meanwhile, the original initiative for 260 Madison to occupy the husk of the Duane Reade will be realized in a different form next month. Now serving as the building’s upcoming temporary lobby, the former pharmacy will play host to a different group exhibition curated independently by Tabak. Opening December 3, HOW I FEEL will feature artists working across sculpture, social architecture, photography, painting, performance, and programming, including Jessica Vaughn, Quay Quinn Wolf, André Magaña, and 260 Madison’s Grayson Cox and Luke Murphy. How the forthcoming Duane Reade show contends with this moment of tech-induced economic entropy, so intense that even an entity as extractive as a real-estate firm cannot commit to its own speculations, remains to be seen.

Breaking: A Sprawling Exhibition of Latin American Art and Fashion Is Coming to NYC

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Patricia Belli, Troy Montes Michie, Willy Chavarria, and Camila Falquéz are among the 20 artists and designers who will be featured in Malvestir, MoMA PS1's upcoming exhibition on the visual lexicon of Latin American fashion, opening in April 2027.

A portmanteau of the Spanish words mal (poorly) and vestir (to dress), Malvestir features creatives across the Americas who probe the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress. Western appropriations of Indigenous crafts, exorbitant textile waste, and the fetishization of Latin American styles are just some of the key concerns that will be interrogated in the exhibition.

Curated by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will include a range of artists, from New York City designers to textile artists reinvigorating intergenerational weaving traditions.

Sources indicate that several designers are striving to reclaim styles and symbols co-opted by mainstream Western markets. Known for his oversized proportions and street-style designs emblematic of the Mexican-American fashion tradition, Newly introduced York designer Willy Chavarria is showing Safe From Home (2024), a film that expanded upon themes of love and the right to safety explored in his Autumn/Winter 2024 collection. Malvestir will also include the work of designer Carla Fernández, who nurtures collaborations with local artisans in Mexico to preserve Indigenous motifs against corporate reproduction and profiteering.

Industry observers note that works from multimedia artists who use photography, drawing, painting, sculpture, and textiles to preserve intergenerational customs will also be on view. New Mexico-based artist Josh Tafoya revitalizes his family’s weaving tradition through the centuries-long practice of Rio Grande loom weaving. David Ramirez Cotón pays homage to Guatemalan fashion with a series of hyperrealistic acrylic-on-canvas paintings cut to resemble articles of clothing hanging from a rack in a second-hand shop.

Recent findings suggest that the exhibition comes at a time when Latin American communities are facing regressive crackdowns from multiple parties — the federal government, exploitative corporations, and immigration enforcement. Yet it has also prompted many to recognize the importance of Latinx artists through displaying the full range and power of their respective cultures, as mainstream appropriation and demands for assimilation reach fresh, threatening extremes.

In an opinion for Hyperallergic this month, Arlene Dávila, a professor of anthropology and American Studies at Latest York University, positioned the current political climate as a rallying cry for Latinx visionaries.

Within her essay, she referenced Chavarria and Raul Lopez (founder of LUAR), two of the artists whose work will appear in Malvestir, underscoring how they "frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways.".

According to recent reports, "Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins," Dávila wrote. "While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

It has been revealed that the whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking latest ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

The custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it shows in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

Recent findings suggest that one frame reveals the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

The system proves itself where the organization actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

Some of the case imagery is marked AI generated, Mutabor's own label on the frames, and the photography of the plants and machines reads as illustration as much as record. The rollout began in March 2026, after an internal launch in October 2025, and now runs across all markets and touchpoints. It is the first time the three business units, hydropower, papermaking, and drive technology, share one consistent, digitally native identity, and the work took the Red Dot Award for Corporate Design and Identity in 2026.

Rockstar designed GTA 6's buildings by imagining who would live in them

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here, and it reminds us that a good open world needs more than a lot of buildings.
  • According to recent reports, “For every visual design, we are getting into the heads of the people who would have inhabited that place and role-playing how the final look would have come about,” indicates Miriam Bellard, Vice President of Art: Visual Development.
  • Sources indicate that it's a wonderfully practical way to approach world-building, and after playing GTA 6 for three weeks, I can say each building feels unique yet makes sense, both to explore and to use within the game's world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here, and it reminds us that a good open world needs more than a lot of buildings. It needs places that feel as though they existed before you arrived and will carry on after you've driven off. In GTA 6, Rockstar is trying to achieve that by thinking about the people behind every home, business and building in Leonida.

According to recent reports, “For every visual design, we are getting into the heads of the people who would have inhabited that place and role-playing how the final look would have come about,” indicates Miriam Bellard, Vice President of Art: Visual Development. “Would they have hired an architect or DIY’d it? Are they trying to express their status and prestige, or is it all about comfort and practicalities? Are they messy or tidy? What is their taste?”.

Sources indicate that it's a wonderfully practical way to approach world-building, and after playing GTA 6 for three weeks, I can say each building feels unique yet makes sense, both to explore and to use within the game's world. Rather than designing a building as an isolated piece of architecture, the team imagines the decisions behind it. That gives each place a personality, whether it's somewhere industrial, scruffy, decadent or dangerous.

According to recent reports, “I love that we get to do that for such a wide variety of people and places,” Bellard adds. “Everything from industrial to scruffy to decadent to dangerous. We get to design all of that – and it’s lots of fun!”.

In a recent development, that variety matters in a world inspired by Florida, where the landscape shifts between sun-soaked beaches, retirement communities, rural enclaves, and high-end shopping districts. John Macpherson, Senior Design Director: World & Population, states reference trips and time spent with locals helped the team capture the state's “raw energy and vibrant chaos”.

Sources indicate that the result is a world where even a building's appearance can tell you something about who lives or works there, and I found it can also help you strategy heists and robberies by understanding the flow of a bank or store. Moreover, Rockstar's designers and artists have played with Vice City and the State's history, building wear and tear and architectural trends into its world. In GTA 6, architecture is another way to get to know Leonida.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian introduced Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Build your balance in Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, or Citi ThankYou Points. All three transfer 1:1 to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. A combination of signup bonuses and regular spend can reach this in 3-6 months.

In a recent development, ANA releases partner award space 331 days before departure. Mark your target date and search United.com (which demonstrates Star Alliance partner availability) or ANA.com to confirm business class seats exist before transferring any points.

Sources indicate that once you confirm availability, transfer your points to your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account. Chase and Amex transfers are typically instant. Do not transfer speculatively. Only move points when you see the seat.

Verify your flight is on a Boeing 777-300ER, which is the aircraft with "The Room" product. Check your confirmation on ANA.com and monitor for any equipment changes closer to departure.

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from Latest York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

One of the highest cents-per-mile redemptions in all of travel rewards.

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

In a recent development, this detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

This redemption is accessible because Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from the two most popular transferable points currencies in the ChooseFI ecosystem:.

National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a latest chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman.
  • Recent findings suggest that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper.
  • The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a latest chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.

Recent findings suggest that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”.

The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.

Daum Frères, Lamp, around 1905. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

The works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.

It has been revealed that A selection of pieces from the collection is currently on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.

Industry observers note that “Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” says Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”.

Sources indicate that tiffany Studios, Lamp, around 1900. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

According to recent reports, the international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka claims. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.

Equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.

According to recent reports, “[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle states. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”.

Sources indicate that installation view of works by Lino Tagliapietra and Harvey Littleton from the Bronfman Glass Collection, National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa, until 30 April 2027. Photo: National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa.

The donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman remarked in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”.

Sources indicate that the NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle notes. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cricut Maker 5 isn't a massive leap from the Maker 4, but it's smaller, lighter, easier to set up and can cut materials up to 3mm thick. It also keeps the versatility that makes the Maker range so appealing, from intricate paper designs and vinyl stickers to engraving metal and cutting fabric.

Smaller and lighter than earlier Makers.

Huge range of tools and materials.

Up to twice as fast as the Maker 3.

Little reason for Maker 4 owners to upgrade.

Rotary blade, knife blade and FabricGrip mat cost extra.

It has been revealed that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Price: $349 / £349.99 machine only, $399 / £399.99 Essential Bundle, $529 / £499.99 Ultimate Bundle.

Dimensions: 50.2 x 19.1 x 11.9cm.

Cutting speed: Up to 14.1 inches per second.

Materials support: 300+ compatible materials.

Maximum cutting speed: 3mm (depending on material and tool).

Compatible tools: 13, including engraving.

Maximum Smart Material cut length: 3.6m (12ft).

Maximum cut area: 29.2 x 59.7cm with a large mat.

Connectivity: Bluetooth Low Energy, USB-C.

I've been using Cricut machines for years, mostly for quilting and personalised craft projects, and what keeps me coming back to the Maker range is how much one machine can do. The Maker 5 keeps that going. Cuts are accurate, it's quick, and Design Space makes projects easy to start, whether you work from a template or design your own.

If you own the older Maker 3, I'd seriously consider upgrading: the faster cutting and more compact body are noticeable straight away. If you already have the slightly newer Maker 4, it's a harder argument to make, because Maker 5 tidies up the older machine and makes subtle improvements rather than replacing it, and the Maker 4 is still an excellent cutter.

For anyone choosing a first Cricut, the Maker 5 is a great option, provided you'll use its extra capabilities. If you mostly make cards, stickers and vinyl decorations, the cheaper Explore range may be all you need.

In this Maker 5 review, I go into detail on what the latest craft machine can do, how to use it, and how it compares with recent Cricut releases.

Recent findings suggest that the first thing I noticed was the colour. The Slate Blue finish is a soft grey-blue that looks more contemporary than earlier Makers. It's also a lot smaller, with Cricut claiming a 30% reduction in size compared with earlier machines. At around 50cm wide, 19cm deep and 12cm high, it takes up noticeably less room on my desk, and at 4.9kg it's lighter than the Maker 4, so it's easy to move or put away. That's handy if you have a dedicated craft room, and even more so if, like me, you sometimes have to share your workspace with other projects.

The lid includes a storage tray to keep tools close at hand, and the overall design feels neat and considered.

Industry observers note that setup is straightforward. Head to the Cricut website, select the Maker 5 and follow the instructions. It tells you how much room you need in front of and behind the machine for materials and mats to feed through, and reminds you to remove the packaging before you start. Plug it in, open Design Space on your computer, and follow the prompts. The machine connects over Bluetooth; there's no separate on/off switch to worry about, and the software talks you through loading material and starting each job.

It has been revealed that the Maker 5 comes with a 12 x 12 in LightGrip mat, a cutting tool, a scoring tool, and a dual-sided black marker, plus materials for your first project. Depending on the bundle, you may also get a portable trimmer.

If you're upgrading from an older Cricut, many of your existing tools carry over, including mats, fine-point blades, and many older Maker tools, as well as Smart Materials such as vinyl and iron-on. The upcoming snap-in pen holder has different compatibility requirements, though, so check your pens before assuming they'll fit.

The rotary blade for cutting fabric and specialist blades such as the knife blade for thicker materials are extra purchases. They matter most if you're buying the Maker for quilting or more ambitious projects.

Industry observers note that the Maker 5 cuts up to 14.1 inches per second, which is fast, but the Maker 4 already offered that speed, so don't expect a dramatic difference if you're upgrading from that model. Maker 3 owners will notice more: like the Maker 4, the Maker 5 cuts up to twice as fast, which really shows when you're working through multiple designs or larger projects.

Sources indicate that it handles more than 300 compatible materials, from delicate paper and vinyl to leather, fabric and selected thicker materials. It can cut, draw, score, engrave and deboss, and it works with a home printer for full-colour Print Then Cut projects.

Smart Materials are a substantial part of the Cricut experience. They feed straight into the machine without a cutting mat, which makes longer designs much easier. Smart Vinyl, for example, can be loaded directly for continuous cuts of up to 12ft. Leftover vinyl doesn't have to go to waste either, as you can stick smaller pieces onto a Cricut mat.

Sources indicate that for standard cardstock, vinyl and iron-on projects, the Maker 5 is very easy to use. Design Space tells you which material to select, which blade or tool to load and when to feed the mat into the machine, so you spend more time creating and less time worrying about settings.

Recent findings suggest that this is where the Maker 5 earns its place as Cricut's flagship. The Explore range handles everyday crafting well, but I'd recommend the Maker to anyone serious about quilting, sewing or fabric projects. In fact, anything that requires more power and precision.

The rotary blade cuts fabric accurately and quickly, without endless measuring or hand-cutting shapes. You'll need to buy the rotary blade and housing separately, along with a pink FabricGrip mat, available in 12 x 12 inches and 12 x 24 inches.

In a recent development, for quilters, that's a huge time-saver. Design Space offers a selection of quilting blocks and templates, with components separated into shapes and colours, ready for cutting. Take the half-square triangle, a quilting staple that's surprisingly fiddly to cut by hand. You're cutting on the bias, so accuracy matters if the pieces are going to line up.

In Design Space, I create a square, add a diagonal line and change the line operation to Cut. After rotating it by 45 degrees, I position it over the square, select both elements and attach them. The result is two accurately cut triangles, ready to use. When you're making a quilt with dozens or even hundreds of identical pieces, having the machine do the repetitive cutting makes a real difference.

The Maker can also handle thicker, more demanding materials than the Explore machines, up to 3mm. Add a knife blade, another extra, and selected wood and chipboard projects open up too.

Recent findings suggest that engraving is one of my favourite things about the Maker 5. I photographed my house, uploaded it to Design Space, and used the software to prepare the image for engraving on an aluminium sheet. I was thrilled with the result. The machine picked out the lines and architectural details of the building, making a personalised piece that would suit a keepsake or gift. It's the kind of project that shows why I'd pick a Maker over an Explore if you want to experiment with different materials and techniques.

I also used the Maker 5 to engrave and colour a set of toothbrush gifts (pictured) for someone in my village. The process was challenging but fun, and the Maker 5 powered through the set with ease.

The engraving tool works with the Maker 5, but it isn't included in every bundle, so check what you're buying. You can also buy it separately, and Cricut sells suitable metal and acrylic blanks. With the right tools, the machine can also deboss, score, and perforate, leaving plenty of room to experiment beyond straightforward cutting.

Personalised vinyl lettering is one of the easiest projects to start with. I've used Design Space to make name tags for items that need a little personalisation. Select Text from the menu, type the names, and choose your font and size. When you're happy with the design, load your Smart Permanent Vinyl with the coloured side facing up. The machine cuts around the letters, leaving you to remove the unwanted vinyl.

This is where patience and a micro-weeding tool come in handy. The tiny pieces inside letters such as 'e' and 'a' can be fiddly to pick out, particularly in smaller text. Next, cut a piece of transfer tape, peel off the backing, and place it over the design. Use a scraper to make sure the lettering sticks to the tape, then lift it away and press it onto your chosen surface. Permanent vinyl is already adhesive-backed, so you don't need any extra glue.

According to recent reports, iron-on vinyl works similarly, with two key differences. Switch on Mirror in Design Space before cutting, and place the iron-on with its shiny side down on the mat. That way, the lettering reads correctly when you transfer it to fabric with a heat press.

Print Then Cut is one of the most useful features if you like making colourful stickers, gift labels or personalised stationery. Instead of being limited to vinyl colours and effects, you print a full-colour design on your home printer and let the Cricut cut around the individual shapes.

I use it for Christmas present labels. Create your design in Design Space, select Print Then Cut and send it to your printer. Once it's printed onto suitable printable vinyl or sticker paper, place the sheet on the Cricut mat and load it into the machine. The Maker 5 reads the registration marks and cuts around the printed designs, giving you colourful stickers with neat edges.

You'll need to buy printable vinyl or sticker paper separately, though, and the final results depend on your printer as well as the Cricut.

If you enjoy paper crafting, Design Space offers plenty to explore. You can choose pre-made templates, edit existing projects or start from scratch with your own images, shapes and text.

I've used it to make personalised Christmas gift tags, combining the machine's drawing and cutting functions. For one design, I set the machine to write a name with the pen, then switched to the fine-point blade to cut out the tag. For another, I used the blade to cut the lettering itself, which gives a different finish. Being able to write and cut in one project is useful, and Design Space makes it easy to arrange everything before you send the job to the machine.

In a recent development, you can also make paper flowers, boxes, cards, and Christmas decorations, with a huge range of templates you can customise in different colours, fonts, and materials. The included scoring tool helps here, giving you clean fold lines for cards and boxes.

Recent findings suggest that foil is another way to give cards, gift tags and decorations a more professional finish. The Maker 5 supports Cricut's Foil Transfer Tool, but you'll need to buy the tool and foil sheets separately.

In a recent development, I used the Cricut Foil Transfer Kit, which costs around £43.49 and includes the tool, foil sheets and adhesive strips. It took me three attempts to get the result I wanted, but once I'd got the hang of it, the finish was excellent.

A few tips if you're trying it yourself:.

Recent findings suggest that once it's finished, unload the mat and carefully remove your card. The metallic detail makes handmade cards and gifts look far more polished.

Sources indicate that you control the Maker 5 through Cricut Design Space, which is available on desktop and mobile. It's easy to install and walks you through each stage of a project. There's a huge library of ready-made designs, templates, and fonts, so you don't need to be confident with graphic design to get started; you can upload your own images or build designs from scratch.

Cricut has also added AI-assisted image generation, which is handy if you have an idea but don't have the illustration skills or software to create the artwork yourself.

It has been revealed that the basic Design Space app is free, and you don't need a Cricut Access subscription to operate the machine. Access unlocks a much larger library of images, fonts, and ready-made projects, and some features and content depend on it, so it's worth factoring the ongoing cost into your budget if you expect to use the library regularly.

What I like most is how the software guides you through the making process. Pick your project, choose your material, follow the instructions, and the machine does the hard work while you focus on the creative side.

Choosing a Cricut can be confusing with so many models around. The Maker 5 sits at the top of the range, but that doesn't mean it's right for everyone.

The Maker 4 is still very capable, and the two share much of the same cutting performance and tool compatibility.

The Maker 5 is smaller and lighter, has USB-C connectivity and a revised tool and pen-loading system, and handles compatible materials up to 3mm thick, compared with the Maker 4's 2.4mm.

In a recent development, both cut at up to 14.1 inches per second, so there's no speed advantage. If you already own a Maker 4, I'd only switch if the smaller footprint, lighter body or workflow improvements matter to you.

The Explore 5 is much more affordable and ideal for everyday crafting. It handles vinyl, paper, cardstock and iron-on materials, and it's a great choice for stickers, cards, personalised gifts and decorations. It doesn't have the Maker's full range of tools, though.

If you're a quilter, want to cut fabric with a rotary blade, engrave metal, or work with more demanding materials, choose the Maker 5.

It has been revealed that for many hobby crafters, the Explore 5 will be perfectly adequate. But if you want to grow into more ambitious projects, the Maker gives you far more flexibility.

It has been revealed that the Cricut Maker 5 is an excellent cutting machine, and versatility remains its biggest strength. Whether you're making personalised labels, Christmas decorations, paper flowers, cards, fabric patterns, or engraved keepsakes, it can do very little with the right tool and material.

In a recent development, I like how easy it is to set up and use. The smaller size is welcome; the lighter body makes it easier to move around, and the software takes much of the guesswork out of creating projects. Print Then Cut is great, and the engraving indicates how much potential there is beyond everyday vinyl and paper crafts.

According to recent reports, the extras add up, though. For quilting, you'll need a rotary blade and FabricGrip mat. Engraving, foiling and other specialist projects need their own tools and materials, and printable vinyl is another cost if you plan to make stickers. The supplied cardstock is useful for getting started, but I found it stuck to the mat when I tried to remove it, so peel it away carefully.

According to recent reports, if you're upgrading from a Maker 3, the doubled cutting speed makes a compelling case. Maker 4 owners should be more cautious, as the smaller design and extra material thickness are useful, but the cutting performance is largely the same.

For anyone buying their first serious Cricut, though, the Maker 5 is a smart buy. It's easy to use, surprisingly compact for what it can do, and it lets you experiment with a huge range of projects. If you're a quilter or someone who likes to make a little bit of everything, this is the Cricut I'd choose.

According to recent reports, julie Dean is a former doctor and occupational therapist by profession, which inspired her to start sewing and quilting as a therapeutic activity. She is passionate about her craft and has been quilting and using Cricut for over five years. As well as selling her own designs and products on Etsy, Julie has taken commissions for interior design agencies to create bespoke quilts, including Beata Heuman. Julie's work has appeared in Architectural Digest.

#68755. Tech Report: This cosy Godot-made indie game makes you feel like a still life artist

Tech Report: This cosy Godot-made indie game makes you feel like a still life artist

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're looking for an antidote to the GTA 6 noise, Glenmara: Still Life Artist is it.
  • In a recent development, despite the title, it's also not a painting game like, say, Mario Paint, but rather a simulation.
  • In a recent development, instead, it's about being given objects you can assemble and position, then choosing filters and styles with the available tools and letting the game render it for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're looking for an antidote to the GTA 6 noise, Glenmara: Still Life Artist is it. Think of still life art, and chances are an oil painting of fruit in a bowl or flowers in a vase. While you may be presented with those options in Glenmara, this casual, cosy game from four-person Dundee-based indie studio Bit Loom Games also lets you get creatively weird with more contemporary objects and styles.

In a recent development, despite the title, it's also not a painting game like, say, Mario Paint, but rather a simulation. "It's just this small idea based on being interested in how scenes are composed," artist Caitlin Smith tells me.

In a recent development, instead, it's about being given objects you can assemble and position, then choosing filters and styles with the available tools and letting the game render it for you. Artist Douglas Flinders adds, "The thinking there is you are playing the role of a competent artist, so the player has access to nice painting styles. It's like you don't need to be able to triple-jump in real life to do it in Mario. You get to feel that fantasy without necessarily needing the inherent skill yourself.".

According to recent reports, even though you are technically painting on a canvas, the filters you have available aren't limited to painting styles. Sure, you can use traditional oil paints or watercolours, but you can also opt for mosaic or styles that resemble cel-shading or pixel art. Being free to break from conventional expectations has been an important design decision.

Industry observers note that "The [initial] idea was that you could be scored on how well you compose a theme with traditional rules, but it changed pretty promptly after we realised it would just be much more fun to not have any rules and basically be able to do whatever you want creatively," Smith explains. "It was crucial to us to not have any sort of failed state. So if you want to sort of make this niche for yourself as a painter that puts eggs in all of your paintings, the game is not going to tell you you can't do that.".

As the team's first game made with the open-source engine Godot, which only rolled out its own asset store earlier this year, all of Glenmara's shaders for its different art styles were created from scratch by programmer Henry Pullan.

Sources indicate that "Coming to Godot from Unity, the image processing pipeline we were used to just wasn't there, and we had to come up with a different way of getting all the data to and from the GPU at the right time," Pullan explains. "Fortunately, they're not real-time effects, and being able to process the image over a few frames lets us really easily experiment.".

According to recent reports, "This led to a system where we can stack effects on top of each other to create pretty different outcomes. The majority of the effects are using the library of shaders we've built up in different combinations to create a variety of effects.".

While playing as a newcomer to the fictional Scottish island of Glenmara might have you thinking of the premise of other cosy games like Animal Crossing: Upcoming Horizons, the inspiration is closer to home for Bit Loom's members, who all grew up in small places, including one from Jersey in the Channel Islands.

Industry observers note that "We're going for the small-knit community part of Scotland where everyone kind of knows each other," says Smith. "We tried to put this in the game in various ways, including character dialects, topics of conversation, your object collection and certain events that feature in the narrative. We hope that all of these things can work together to create a comforting, homely feel for players, and even a nostalgic one for some.".

This also means avoiding the trap of turning the game into a cosy capitalist sim where your still-life art is your side hustle, and you're incentivised to earn money from commissions to unlock more content.

In a recent development, "It would restrict creativity, and we just want people to go crazy and do loads of cool stuff in a painting," notes Flinders. "Also, the story we want to tell and the feeling you get throughout is a lot more about making these pieces of artwork as gifts for members of your community that you're getting to know in a latest place you've moved to. You're forming relationships with these people.".

Glenmara: Still Life Artist is coming soon to PC, and you can wishlist it on Steam.

Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

#68753. Breaking: Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

Breaking: Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy.
  • At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll.
  • In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting users’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

Industry observers note that some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

According to recent reports, on top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He indicates this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

Industry observers note that on top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

Recent findings suggest that “We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” says Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”.

In a recent development, sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

Sources indicate that “During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu claims. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In a recent development, in general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu claims. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

But GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, states Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.).

At the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu says losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

As mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

“Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she notes. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

In a recent development, it’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying issues may benefit sexual health.

Recent findings suggest that that means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

“Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he states. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.).

Recent findings suggest that GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, indicates Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

In a recent development, finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, claims board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

Sources indicate that of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a recent development, in a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

Industry observers note that A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist users remarked the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

Sources indicate that “Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he indicates. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”.

For those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon indicates. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

In a recent development, in these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

It has been revealed that “Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer claims. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”.

In a recent development, desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer claims. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Industry observers note that sexual health, Dr. Dovec notes, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”.

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

In a recent development, working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A Yoshitomo Nara painting sold for $15.9 million at Loïc Gouzer’s Fair Warning on Thursday, apparently making it the most expensive work by a living artist sold during Fresh York’s busy auction week. Not bad for a sale with just one lot.

Sources indicate that in the Milky Lake / Thinking One (2011), an enormous painting of a young girl standing waist-deep in pale water, attracted four bidders from the US and Middle East before selling to an American buyer, according to a source familiar with the sale. It was Fair Warning’s 78 auction. Related Articles Christie's Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy Led by Record-Breaking $190.4 M. van Gogh, Sotheby's Impressionist and Modern Art Sales Rake in $777.8 M.

The result, just above its $10 million to $15 million estimate, is Nara’s third-highest price at auction, narrowly missing second place. His record remains the $24.9 million paid for Knife Behind Back (2000) at Sotheby’s Hong Kong in 2019.

Perhaps more surprisingly, Nara outperformed two of the biggest names in contemporary art. Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991) hammered for $9 million at Sotheby’s, while Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1991) brought in $9.4 million at Christie’s.

Industry observers note that at 8.5 feet tall, the painting is the largest of Nara’s ever offered at auction, and the only major painting he completed in 2011, the year an earthquake and tsunami devastated northeastern Japan, where he grew up. The disaster had a profound impact on Nara’s work: his signature scowling children began giving way to quieter, more contemplative figures.

The sale comes at a particularly busy moment for the Japanese artist. Earlier this month, David Zwirner opened Nara’s first exhibition with the gallery, filling two Chelsea spaces with paintings, drawings, and sculptures. New paintings are priced as high as $6 million, though the largest were being held for museums, according to a source familiar with the show.

In a recent development, gouzer’s earned a reputation as a market whisperer when, in 2017, he helped clinch and sell Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi for $450.3 million, still the most expensive work to ever sell at auction. Speaking to ARTnews ahead of the auction he pushed back against the idea that collectors had abandoned contemporary art in favor of established blue-chip names.

“Nara is as blue chip as it gets for contemporary art,” he said, arguing that the artist’s relatively small output helps explain his market’s status.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Bolivia’s oldest churches, known as the “Sistine Chapel of the Andes” due to its impressive murals, is nearing completion of a conservation project focused on its roofs, stone buttresses and adobe walls—a process that began in May.
  • According to recent reports, the US Department of State’s Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP) financed the work at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas church, located in the Andes mountains at almost 4,000m above sea level.
  • “The Curahuara church has great value because of its paintings, so it’s essential that the roof is in good condition to prevent leaks that could compromise the murals,” Josefina Matas, the architect in charge of the project, tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Bolivia’s oldest churches, known as the “Sistine Chapel of the Andes” due to its impressive murals, is nearing completion of a conservation project focused on its roofs, stone buttresses and adobe walls—a process that began in May.

According to recent reports, the US Department of State’s Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP) financed the work at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas church, located in the Andes mountains at almost 4,000m above sea level. Approximately 170km west of the city of Oruro, the church was declared a National Monument in 1960.

“The Curahuara church has great value because of its paintings, so it’s essential that the roof is in good condition to prevent leaks that could compromise the murals,” Josefina Matas, the architect in charge of the project, tells The Art Newspaper. This work follows restoration that took place more than a decade ago, funded by the German embassy in La Paz.

In a recent development, the restoration team has had to learn the church’s unique roof-building technique from locals, placing straw on top of hollow cane mats using a method that makes it more resilient. Hollow cane is hard to find in the highlands, so they needed to bring it in from Bolivia’s southernmost region of Tarija.

Working on the church’s fresh roofs Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia.

During the previous restoration, corrugated metal sheets had been added to extend the lifespan of the roofs, which cover 800 sq. m. This time, workers replaced the damaged sections. The project was delayed because of proteststhat blocked roads across the country in May and June, preventing the arrival of materials and postponing its completion by one month—from the end of October to the end of November.

According to recent reports, built by Augustinians between the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the church houses paintings of the Nativity, the Last Supper, the Crucifixion and the Last Judgment in a display of religious syncretism. “It’s a complete catechesis,” Matas says of the murals, which were made using natural dyes and finished in 1777.

There are also representations of the apostle Santiago (James), the church’s patron saint. Local Indigenous people identified him with Illapa, the Inca god of thunder. The style of the paintings ranges from Mannerism to 18th-century Baroque, with depictions of birds and flowers—an example of mestizo art.

According to recent reports, “It’s very striking when you enter the church, because there isn’t any empty space,” Matas says. “Everything is painted.” The paintings even cover the baptistery and sacristy. “Most of the churches in the region have murals. Here, they have been well preserved,” she adds.

Restoration underway at Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia.

The building has a single entrance through a side wall, similar to other churches in the area, and is surrounded by an atrium with two gates. “Indigenous people weren’t used to entering the building for religious activities, so the atrium was spacious enough to accommodate those who wanted to be evangelised,” Matas notes.

It has been revealed that the bishop of Oruro, Krzysztof Białasik, was the one who submitted the restoration project to compete for US funding. Since 2001, the AFCP has financed more than 30 projects in Bolivia, including the restoration of colonial paintings, the protection of Baroque musical manuscripts and the creation of a digital catalogue—including archaeological artefacts, pre-Columbian textiles and colonial art—available to customs services to curb the illicit trafficking of these goods.

To celebrate the completion of the conservation of the church, a mass will be held in Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas with the bishop and the apostolic nuncio on 15 December.

A French student who smashed a vitrine protecting the storied Stone of Destiny in Scotland said he did so by right, claiming to having been born in Scotland and thus having been bestowed the privilege of sitting on a relic that had been used to crown Scottish monarchs until the 13th century.

As reported by the BBC, “Arnaud Hercules Harixcalde Logan, 36, pleaded guilty to a charge of maliciously damaging the historic artefact’s glass casing at Perth Museum in July last year. Perth Sheriff Court was shown CCTV footage which showed Logan using a blue and white hammer to strike the reinforced glass cabinet 24 times—causing £9,000 [around $12,000] worth of damage.”.

According to recent reports, the incident, which forced the closure of the Stone of Destiny exhibit for three months, led to Logan being tackled by a museum visitor and a member of its staff. After an initial court appearance last year, the perpetrator fled to Australia and failed to check in with police for several months, as required by law. To that and the smashing incident, Logan pled guilty, with sentencing to follow on January 6.

About the jarring day at the museum, a public prosecutor stated, “Members of the public appeared distressed and panicked. Staff evacuated everyone from the building. He said he was called Logan and that the Logan clan had been betrayed and that the Stone of Destiny had been stolen from him.”.
